transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. I'm just... I'm at my wit's end, to be completely honest with you. What brings me in is that I just can't seem to keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. And it's not just the mundane stuff, it's happening even when it's incredibly important. 

I'm a computer support specialist, so a lot of my job is highly technical, digging into systems when things go wrong. Just the other day, for example, I had this major client whose whole system was bottlenecking, so I sat down to trace the network problem. I pulled up the server logs, which is standard procedure, you know, looking for the dropped packets or the error codes. But I'll be sitting there, staring at the screen, and ten minutes later I'll suddenly realize that I've just reread the exact same block of log entries three times. Three times! And I still don't know what they actually say. 

It's like my eyes are scanning the text, the IP addresses, the timestamps, but absolutely nothing is registering in my brain. And then I have to start all over again, which is incredibly frustrating when you have an entire office waiting on you to fix their connection so they can get back to work. It's just... it's like my brain just unplugs itself right in the middle of a thought, and I don't even notice until I've wasted ten minutes staring at a monitor. It's really starting to scare me, because I have a graduate degree, I know how to do this work, I've been doing it for years, but now I just sit there spinning my wheels.
Did you have similar problems with attention or staying focused when you were a child?

Oh, wow, yes. Actually... it's funny you ask that, because my mother—she's 82 now, bless her—she still brings this up at family gatherings. It's like her favorite running joke. She kept all my old report cards from grade school in this big plastic tub in her attic, and she loves to remind me what the teachers used to write on them, year after year. 

She says every single one of them, from like first grade all the way through middle school, basically had the exact same comments. They always started by saying I was a bright kid, you know, that I was smart and had a lot of potential, which I guess was their polite way of softening the blow for my parents. Because right after that, in the little notes section at the bottom, they'd write about how I absolutely never stayed in my seat. I mean, I remember just feeling this... this physical need to get up and wander around the classroom. I'd go look out the window, or go sharpen my pencil for the fifth time, or just walk over to see what the kid three desks down was doing. 

And then there was the talking. The report cards always, always mentioned that I blurted out answers. I just couldn't wait to be called on. The teacher would ask a math question or something, and the answer would pop into my head, and it was like my mouth just bypassed my brain's filter entirely. I'd just shout it out before anyone else could even raise their hand, which used to drive my teachers absolutely up the wall. 

But the worst part, and the thing that really used to frustrate me back then, was the homework. My mom jokes about it now, but man, I would spend hours doing my worksheets or writing a book report at the kitchen table. I knew I did it. My mom watched me do it. And then I'd get to school the next day, the teacher would call for the assignments, I'd open my backpack, and it was just... gone. I lost my homework all the time, even when I had definitely, one hundred percent finished it the night before. It was like a black hole in my folder. So, yeah, I guess looking back, this isn't exactly a brand new problem, even if it feels so much more catastrophic now with my career on the line...
